paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Anderson took place at Leesburg, Virginia, on the night of August 12-13, 1920, when Loudoun County residents stormed the county jail to seize Anderson, a Black man held on a charge of attempting to attack a young white woman. Sheriff Edwards and his deputies held the crowd off, and on the direction of Governor Westmoreland Davis, Anderson was taken to the jail at Winchester, where militia were kept ready. White papers in Washington, Richmond, Birmingham and Chattanooga carried the story as a short news item, and the Richmond Planet, a Black weekly, reprinted the Richmond account a week later.

Anderson was described as about twenty-five years old and a Loudoun County man whose father lived at Purcellville. According to a Leesburg dispatch in the Washington Times, the woman, whom it named "Mrs. Arthur Bridler," said a man slipped up behind her as she shelled peas on her front porch at Belmont Park and struck her on the head with a rock before her cries frightened him off. Other papers named her Mrs. Virginia Cridler, nineteen, and the Times-Dispatch called her "a bride of three months" and placed the alleged attempt near Goose Creek, on her way to a store. The Washington Herald reported the charge as "criminal assault," while the other accounts spoke of an attempted attack.

A posse of 150 citizens led by Sheriff Edwards caught Anderson within forty minutes of the alleged attack on August 12 and placed him in the Leesburg jail, amid "some talk of mob violence." That night, according to the Times-Dispatch's Winchester correspondent, county residents stormed the jail and demanded that Anderson be turned over to them and lynched. The Herald said the assault went on "all night" and that the sheriff, his guards and deputies fought off the mob, which the Times-Dispatch said "apparently lacked a leader." Neither account reported anyone hurt.

When Sheriff Edwards heard lynching talk again the next afternoon, he conferred with Governor Davis at the governor's home in Leesburg, and they decided to take Anderson out of the county. Sheriff Pannett of Frederick County agreed to receive the prisoner, and late on August 13 Edwards brought Anderson to Winchester under heavy guard, where he was locked in a steel cage. Local militiamen at Winchester were told to be ready for a call in case of further attempts.

Officials planned to keep Anderson at Winchester until the next term of the Loudoun County Circuit Court. Anderson denied his guilt but otherwise refused to discuss the case with Sheriff Pannett. No report of arrests among the mob, of an indictment or of a trial appears in the coverage.

The Washington Times broke the story on August 13 under the headline "Posse Takes Alleged Assailant of Woman," telling it mainly from the accuser's account and mentioning a mob only in its last line. On August 14 the Washington Herald and the Richmond Times-Dispatch ran special dispatches from Winchester, the first headed "Virginia Jail Under Guard" and the second "Loudoun Citizens Storm County Jail for Negro." A shorter wire version ran among the Chattanooga News's national briefs and in the Birmingham Age-Herald under the headline "Just a Little Late."

The Times-Dispatch, while reporting the mob's demand plainly, described Anderson as "inclined to be surly," passed on Sheriff Edwards's claim that Anderson's father had threatened to blow up Purcellville if his son was prosecuted, and said the Andersons were regarded as "bad men" in the county. The Herald gave the father's threat a different condition, saying it applied "if any violence is done his son." The only Black-press item found was in the Richmond Planet, which on August 21 reprinted the Times-Dispatch dispatch nearly word for word under the headline "Loudon Citizens Storm Jail," keeping the "surly" and "bad men" lines and adding no comment.

The wire account had Anderson removed secretly at night while the mob surrounded the jail, whereas both Winchester specials, which agree with each other and give more detail, placed the removal late the following day. The Washington Times dispatch was itself inconsistent, dating the capture "yesterday" but the alleged attack "this morning."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Anderson
bases: A crowd stormed the Leesburg jail to take a Black prisoner accused of attacking a white woman and have him 'lynched', and was held off by the sheriff (A2, A3, A5).

A mob of Loudoun County citizens tried to seize Anderson from jail to lynch him over an accusation of attacking a white woman, but the sheriff held them off and he was moved to Winchester alive (A2, A3, A5); this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
Two separate special dispatches from Winchester (A2, A3) and an independent wire report (A4, A5) agree that a mob besieged the Leesburg jail and that Anderson was moved to Winchester for safekeeping.

accounts.label: Winchester special correspondents
accounts.gist: Citizens stormed the Leesburg jail all night demanding Anderson to lynch him; the sheriff fought them off, and after renewed lynching talk the next afternoon and a conference with the governor he took Anderson to Winchester.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Anderson was secretly taken from the jail at night while a mob intent on lynching him surrounded it, on the governor's direction.

accounts.label: Sheriff's claims
accounts.gist: Sheriff Edwards said Anderson's father had threatened to blow up Purcellville if his son was prosecuted; the Andersons were called 'bad men'.

framing.detail: Washington Times: 'Posse Takes Alleged Assailant of Woman', the capture by 150 citizens told from the accuser's account, with a closing line on 'talk of mob violence'.
Washington Herald: 'Virginia Jail Under Guard', troops ready 'to Prevent Mob Violence'; calls the citizens 'Infuriated'.
Times-Dispatch reports the lynching demand plainly but describes Anderson as 'inclined to be surly' and the Andersons as 'bad men', and calls the accuser a 'young bride'.
Age-Herald runs the wire under the headline 'Just a Little Late', casting the story from the side of the mob that missed its prisoner.
Chattanooga News runs the same wire item among national briefs.
Richmond Planet reprints the Times-Dispatch dispatch a week later, including the 'surly' and 'bad men' lines, with no comment.
